description: Ulaanbaatar team taking on "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" Mongolia is warming faster than most of the planet, deserts are spreading, and winters bring dzud and smog. We're building a bilingual (Mongolian/English) tool where anyone picks a NASA variable and a region, sees decades of data, and tests whether the trend is real. We're strong in research, design and storytelling.
summary:
Every herder in Mongolia has a story about how the weather has changed: hotter summers, milder winters, a later first frost. But is it really happening in their own soum, or were the last few years just unusual? National averages can’t answer that, and raw satellite charts are hard to read without training in statistics.
 Quindecim answers it at the aimag (province) and soum (district) level. Choose any of Mongolia’s 337 soums and ask one of five questions: Is the land getting greener or drier? Are summers hotter? Are winters milder? Does the first frost come later? Quindecim pulls 25 to 45 years of NASA data for that soum (MODIS for greenness, FLDAS for rainfall and temperature, NASA POWER for frost dates) and replies in one plain sentence: real trend, possible trend, or not proven.
 Behind those simple statements, Quindecim runs careful statistics: each soum is tested with a Mann-Kendall test adjusted for the way one year carries into the next, and every result is checked against chance across all 337 soums, so a lucky streak is never mistaken for real change. Even with these strict checks, we found that summers have truly warmed since 1982 in 197 soums, by about 2 °C in a typical one. Decisions about pasture, water and herds are made locally, so Quindecim gives herders, students, teachers and local officials honest evidence about their own homeland, in Mongolian or English, ready to share on Facebook or Messenger in a few taps.
details:
What does it do?
Quindecim answers one question for every area in Mongolia: is the climate here really changing, or is it just a few unusual years? “Area” means all 337 soums and Ulaanbaatar districts (328 soums plus 9 districts).

  • Pick one of five questions: is it getting greener or browner, wetter or drier, are summers hotter, are winters milder or colder, does the first autumn frost come later?
  • See the map: all 21 aimags and Ulaanbaatar are shaded by the direction and size of their trend. Tap an aimag to see its soums, and tap a soum for its own result.
  • Read the answer in one plain sentence, for example: “Summer greenness in Sergelen has risen about 54% since 2001. This is very unlikely to be chance.” Below it are the yearly values, the trend line and the full test results.
  • See the whole country at a glance: how many areas have a real trend, and where the largest changes are.
  • Share any result as a link or as an image made for Facebook and Messenger, and download the numbers as CSV for one place or all 337 areas.
  • Get info on herding tips and stories of other locals. Quindecim also provides the Discover section where users can learn relevant info to better their knowledge.
  • Use it in English or Mongolian; one tap switches everything, shared images included.

How does it work?

  1. NASA data for every area: with Google Earth Engine we exported MODIS MOD13A2 NDVI (2001-2026, June to August) and FLDAS Noah rainfall and air temperature (1982-2026) for all 337 areas. The first autumn frost (1981-2026) comes from NASA POWER daily minimum temperature at the grid cell of each area’s centre; neighbouring areas can share a cell.
  2. Honest inputs: greenness is measured over grassland only, using the same MODIS MCD12Q1 land-cover pixels every year, so a trend can never come from a change in which land is measured. Only complete seasons are used.
  3. A test for every place: each soum and aimag is tested with the Mann-Kendall trend test, corrected for year-to-year correlation (Hamed and Rao 1998). Sen’s slope gives the rate, and a straight-line fit with an effective sample size (Santer et al. 2000) gives a second opinion.
  4. A check for chance: testing 337 areas at once would produce about 17 false “trends” by luck alone, so every result also faces the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate across all areas. A trend is called real only if it passes both checks (p and q below 0.05).
  5. Plain words: every result becomes one sentence and a verdict (real trend, possible trend or not proven). On the map only real trends get solid colour; possible ones are striped and unproven ones are pale.
  6. Verified: our JavaScript statistics agree with SciPy-based Python reference code to within 0.0000001 on every number we compare (Mann-Kendall, Hamed-Rao, Sen’s slope, the straight-line fit and the false discovery rate).

What did we find?

  • Summers have really warmed in 197 of 337 areas since 1982, by about 2 °C in a typical one, and no area has cooled.
  • Summer greenness on grassland has really risen in 117 of 333 areas since 2001, and none has really browned. It follows the rain: greenness and summer rainfall rise together in 332 of 333 areas, so much of the greening is recovery after the dry early 2000s.
  • Summer rainfall has really fallen in 11 areas and risen in 7; elsewhere the change could still be chance.
  • Winter temperature and the date of the first frost show no trend that passes the check for chance yet.
  • We checked the model against 10 NOAA weather stations. Summer temperatures match well (correlation 0.73 to 0.96, median 0.93), but the model warms less than the stations (+0.2 to +0.5 °C per decade, against +0.5 to +0.8), so we may understate summer warming. Winters in the model are too mild (about 3 °C at the median station), so we do not read winter trends from it.

What benefits does it have?

  • Herders and families: evidence and information about their own soum, in Mongolian, on a phone, instead of a national average.
  • Teachers and students: a real example of how scientists tell a trend from noise, with the full numbers one tap away.
  • Local officials and researchers: a consistent, tested picture of all 337 areas, downloadable as CSV.
  • Everyone: results that are easy to pass on, as a picture for Facebook and Messenger, where Mongolian communities share news.

What do we hope to achieve?
In the short term, we want to put Quindecim in front of teachers, students and soum offices and improve it with their feedback. In the long term, we want to add more NASA variables, such as snow cover and soil moisture, use finer-resolution data so a soum is not limited by a model grid cell, and extend the weather-station check to every soum that has a station.

Furthermore, we want to test our satellite trends on the ground. We plan to request NAMEM’s rangeland monitoring data from its 1,516 sites and its weather station records, then compare each soum’s greenness trend with nearby ground measurements. Where a station is close, its temperatures and frost dates would replace our coarse 10 to 50 km model estimates. Ground records of grazing would also let us begin to separate grazing pressure from climate as causes of change, which satellites alone cannot do. Alongside this, we plan to pilot Quindecim with schools and soum offices in one aimag, and add a printable one-page report for each soum.

What tools did we use?

  • Data and processing: Google Earth Engine (Python API), the NASA POWER API, NOAA GHCN-Daily station records (for the check), Python.
  • Statistics: our own JavaScript code, checked against SciPy and NumPy.
  • Web: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks or libraries; SVG for the map and charts; Canvas for the share images.
  • Design and hosting: Mongolian ornament tiles, the Montserrat typeface, hosted on Vercel.

What makes it creative?
It gives non-experts honest statistics. Most climate apps show a chart and let you guess; Quindecim tells you how sure you can be and never overstates: a large change that could be chance never looks dramatic on the map. It speaks the user’s language, works on a slow phone connection, and turns any result into a picture people actually share.

What did we consider?
Statistical honesty (year-to-year correlation, testing many areas at once, complete seasons, the same grassland every year); slow connections and phones (the page works before the data arrives, and the data is about 260 KB compressed); discover section to equip users with further knowledge; two languages, with nothing moving on the page when you switch; and clear limits: straight-line trends only, neighbouring soums share weather, regional model data is coarser than a soum, the model’s winters are too mild, and a trend is not a cause.

Use of SI
We used SI tools to work faster, but not to replace our own work. A coding assistant (Claude) helped write and debug the code, video editing assistant (Claude). The team chose the questions, the NASA data and the statistical methods, checked every statistic against independent code, and reviewed all results. The Mongolian text is being written by a native speaker. No NASA branding was used or modified.
